5.1.intro: Employers often use several steps because no single document reveals everything. A recruiter may check eligibility and availability, a manager may discuss examples of work, and a work sample may show how someone approaches a task. Stages differ by role, employer and country.
5.1.example: Northstar's process: application review → short recruiter call → work-sample task → manager conversation → decision. A small store might skip all but one conversation.
5.1.language: What are the next steps in the hiring process?
5.1.watch: An interview is not always a numbered round; screening, behavioral and technical questions can be combined.

5.2.intro: Applicant tracking systems help employers store, search and manage applications. Some automatically filter on employer-defined rules; others assist ranking or matching. A résumé should be clearly organized and honest. There is no secret keyword formula that guarantees a human will read it.
5.2.example: A posting requires a particular license. If the form asks whether you hold it, answer accurately. Relevant job terms help describe your experience, but repeating a term many times does not create the underlying skill.
5.2.language: I have experience with the duties listed in your advertisement.
5.2.watch: Do not confuse application software with universal AI rejection. The workflow varies by employer.

5.3.intro: Hiring communication has a simple goal: make it easy for both sides to coordinate and understand the next step. Read the whole message, answer actual questions, confirm dates and reply at an appropriate level of formality. Brief, clear English usually works best.
5.3.example: Recruiter: “Are you available for a 20-minute call on Thursday at 3 p.m.?” Applicant: “Thank you for the invitation. Thursday at 3 p.m. works for me. I look forward to speaking with you.”
5.3.language: Thank you for your message. I can confirm ...
5.3.watch: Never assume an unverified sender is genuine. Confirm suspicious links through official channels.

5.4.intro: An initial screening call usually checks basic fit: availability, relevant experience, interest, work eligibility and sometimes salary expectations. It is often short. Prepare a concise introduction and honest answers to practical questions; do not deliver a memorized autobiography.
5.4.example: Recruiter: “Can you work evening shifts?” Maya: “Yes, I am available on weekdays after 4 p.m., except Tuesdays.” Clear constraints are more helpful than a vague “any time.”
5.4.language: I am available on ... / My notice period is ...
5.4.watch: Some screening calls also include behavioral or technical questions. Ask what to expect.

5.5.intro: An invitation needs a clear confirmation. Check time zone, location or meeting link, length, interview type and required materials. If you cannot attend, propose specific alternatives promptly and politely.
5.5.example:
Subject: Re: Interview invitation
Thank you for inviting me. I can attend on Monday at 10:00 a.m. JST. Could you confirm whether the meeting is online? I look forward to speaking with you.
5.5.language: Would it be possible to reschedule for Tuesday afternoon?
5.5.watch: Never leave a confirmed meeting unanswered if a conflict arises.

5.6.intro: After an initial call, an employer may request a work sample, another conversation, references or a practical assessment. Ask about expectations and reasonable preparation time. Waiting between stages is normal; continue other applications unless you have agreed otherwise.
5.6.example: Northstar asks a support applicant to write a reply to an unhappy customer. A developer might debug a small example. Both tasks can reveal reasoning and communication.
5.6.language: Could you clarify the expected format and deadline for the task?
5.6.watch: Be cautious about unusually large unpaid assignments, especially work that appears commercially usable.

5.7.intro: A thank-you email after an interview is optional in many settings, but a short note can confirm interest and appreciation. Refer to something real from the conversation; do not send a long sales pitch or demand a decision.
5.7.example:
Subject: Thank you for today's interview
Hello Jordan,
Thank you for speaking with me today about the Support Assistant role. I appreciated learning how the team handles difficult cases. The conversation strengthened my interest. Best regards, Maya
5.7.language: Thank you for taking the time to speak with me.
5.7.watch: Follow local conventions and recruiter guidance; a thank-you note is not a guaranteed advantage.

5.8.intro: When no decision arrives, check the timeline you were given. If it has passed, one concise follow-up may be appropriate. Ask for an update without accusing the recruiter. If they remain silent, continue your search.
5.8.example:
Subject: Follow-up — Support Assistant
Hello Jordan,
I hope you're well. I wanted to check whether there is an update on the Support Assistant process. I remain interested. Thank you for your time.
Best, Maya
5.8.language: I wanted to check whether there is an update on my application.
5.8.watch: Repeated messages usually add pressure, not information. Silence is not necessarily a statement about your worth.

5.9.intro: Rejection means the employer will not proceed with this application, not that your abilities have been objectively measured. Some notices are automatic and need no reply. When a person has invested time or invited future contact, a short gracious response can preserve a professional relationship.
5.9.example:
Hello Jordan,
Thank you for letting me know and for the chance to meet your team. I enjoyed our conversation and would welcome consideration for relevant future openings. I wish you all the best.
Maya
5.9.language: Thank you for informing me. I appreciate your time.
5.9.watch: You may be a strong alternate candidate, but there is no reason to assume the offer will come back. Avoid angry replies or pleading.

5.10.intro: An offer is a proposal, not an order. Review the role, compensation, benefits, location, working time, start date, contract terms and any conditions. Compare these with your needs and eligibility before accepting. Questions and negotiations can be appropriate when expressed respectfully.
5.10.example: “Thank you for the offer. Could you clarify the expected weekly hours and whether overtime is paid?” is a decision question, not an insult.
5.10.language: Thank you for the offer. Could I clarify a few details before deciding?
5.10.watch: A mission you admire cannot replace fair and workable terms. Obtain significant terms in writing.

5.11.intro: Accepting, declining and withdrawing are all professional decisions. Be clear, prompt and respectful once you have decided. Keep relationships open where genuine, but do not make promises you cannot keep.
5.11.example: Decline: “Thank you for offering me the position. After careful consideration, I have decided not to accept. I appreciate your time and wish the team well.” Accept: “I'm pleased to accept the offer, subject to the terms in the attached agreement.”
5.11.language: Thank you for the offer. After careful consideration, ...
5.11.watch: Before accepting, confirm the precise terms; avoid withdrawing by simply disappearing.
